strengths: Soundness: The paper presents a coherent latent-space transformer GAN and evaluates four model capacities. FID improves monotonically from 15.24 (S) to 4.02 (XL) at 50K iterations, while the longer-trained XL model reaches a strong FID of 3.02 without guidance and 2.96 with latent-space guidance.

The proposed multi-level noise-perturbed guidance is intuitive and supported by complementary evidence: FID ablations, intermediate-feature visualizations, and a 10K-sample block-removal LPIPS analysis. Comparisons with no MNG, linear scheduling, and resize-based MSG supervision are useful.

The width-dependent learning-rate adjustment is simple and practically relevant. Cross-scale learning-rate swaps demonstrate the expected slow convergence or instability, although they do not fully validate the proposed rule.

Significance and originality: Combining latent GAN training with plain transformer generator/discriminator backbones is useful, and the intermediate noise hierarchy is a reasonably original adaptation of multi-level supervision. Single-step ImageNet generation at the reported quality could be important.

Presentation is generally clear and visually polished. The appendix reports model dimensions, parameter counts, learning rates, optimization settings, noise schedules, compute resources, training curves, uncurated samples, and interpolation examples.
weaknesses: The central scalability claim is under-supported. Results cover only one dataset and resolution, four jointly changed width/depth configurations, and six points in the FLOPs correlation. There is no scaling-law fit, held-out prediction, iso-compute comparison, data scaling, or evidence across datasets/resolutions. A correlation of -0.95 among these hand-selected configurations does not by itself establish general scalability.

The learning-rate rule is justified only heuristically and tested mainly through an S/B cross-swap. The paper does not compare its inverse-width exponent with alternatives, independently tune each scale to establish an oracle optimum, or report corresponding L/XL controls. Consequently, the evidence does not establish that the formula reliably replaces scale-specific tuning.

The computational-efficiency account is incomplete. MNG appears to send four intermediate fake images and four real copies through the discriminator, which could substantially increase discriminator-side cost, yet the paper calls its overhead negligible without reporting throughput or total training FLOPs. Figure 3 counts only one generator forward pass, and epoch-based comparisons ignore the large model, discriminator, frozen DINOv2 feature extraction, and other per-step costs.

The headline comparison is not fully fair or precisely framed. GAT is placed under “GANs from scratch” despite depending on a pretrained Stable-Diffusion VAE and DINOv2-B semantic supervision, while StyleGAN-XL is specially flagged for pretrained-discriminator use. The best 2.96 result also uses latent-space guidance; the unguided result is 3.02. Training compute and matched-resource comparisons are unavailable for most baselines.

Important empirical uncertainty is missing: all quantitative results appear to be single runs, with no seed variation, confidence intervals, stability/failure rates, or statistical testing. Evaluation relies almost exclusively on FID, without precision/recall, density/coverage, or other evidence separating fidelity from diversity. This is especially limiting for GANs and for claims about reliable scaling.

Reproducibility is inadequate for the central results. No code or release commitment is given, and details such as MNG sample aggregation in the discriminator, exact adversarial reduction, augmentation policy, weight decay, FID implementation/statistics, and several initialization and scheduling choices remain unclear. More seriously, Eq. 9 defines REPA as positive cosine similarity while Eq. 10 adds it to a minimized discriminator objective; as written this encourages anti-alignment unless an unstated negative sign is intended.

Presentation contains consequential ambiguities and smaller inconsistencies: the treatment of the K outputs in Eqs. 1–3 is underspecified, the text refers to Fig. 6 although the relevant panel is Fig. 7, and qualitative claims about coarse-to-fine behavior are stronger than what PCA visualizations alone establish.

There is no dedicated limitations or research-ethics discussion. The paper does not address ImageNet bias/licensing, misuse and memorization risks of generative models, or environmental costs, despite reporting a largest run of roughly 12 days on eight RTX A6000 GPUs. These omissions reduce the completeness of the submission but are not the primary reason for rejection.

strengths: The paper tackles an important question—whether latent-space, transformer-based GANs can scale reliably—and reports a strong ImageNet-256 result: FID 3.02 without guidance and 2.96 with latent-space guidance after 40 epochs. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/review_sample501_han_medium_20260920T175328Z/scratch/d1ecf2304fce4a428e44d919d2a2d511/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The proposed MNG mechanism is simple and plausibly useful. Its evaluation includes comparisons against no intermediate guidance, resize-based MSG guidance, and linear versus exponential noise schedules, as well as a 10K-image block-ablation analysis using LPIPS.

The experiments include several informative analyses beyond the headline FID: four model capacities, two patch sizes, separate generator/discriminator scaling, training curves, latent interpolations, and intermediate-feature visualizations.

The appendix provides model dimensions, parameter counts, learning rates, regularization coefficients, optimizer settings, noise levels, precision, batch size, and compute resources, giving a useful partial basis for reproduction.
weaknesses: Soundness: the evidence does not establish the central claim of GAN "scalability" in a rigorous sense. The study uses only ImageNet-256, four capacity points, essentially one training budget, and apparently one run per condition. Larger models obtaining lower FID at fixed iterations is encouraging but is not a scaling law; there are no fitted trends, uncertainty estimates, repeated seeds, held-out predictions, or controlled compute/data scaling experiments.

The width-aware learning-rate rule is insufficiently justified. The informal argument that update magnitude is proportional to learning rate times channel dimension does not derive the output change of the full transformer under AdamW. Experimentally, the rule is tested primarily by swapping the S and B learning rates; this shows that two substantially different learning rates behave differently, but does not demonstrate that inverse-width scaling is uniquely appropriate, robust over a neighborhood, or effective for L and XL without tuning.

The headline comparison is not adequately controlled. GAT uses a pretrained Stable Diffusion VAE and a frozen DINOv2-B teacher, yet Table 1 labels it as trained "from scratch" and discounts StyleGAN-XL because that method uses an ImageNet-pretrained discriminator. This asymmetry materially weakens both the state-of-the-art claim and the fairness of the comparison. There is also no matched-recipe comparison with a strong modern convolutional GAN.

The claimed training/data efficiency is supported mainly by epoch counts. GAT-XL uses roughly 602M generator and 468M discriminator parameters, invokes DINOv2 during training, and requires about 12 days on eight RTX A6000 GPUs. Training FLOPs, throughput, and total accelerator-hours for baselines are absent, while the scaling plot counts only a generator forward pass. Consequently, "6× fewer epochs" should not be interpreted as 6× lower computation.

Evaluation relies almost entirely on FID. There are no precision/recall or coverage measurements, Inception Score, statistical variation, memorization checks, or quantitative latency/throughput results. These omissions are especially important because the paper claims fidelity, coverage, stability, data efficiency, and inference efficiency. The guided 2.96 result also differs only marginally from the unguided 3.02 result.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite the useful appendix. No code or artifact is identified; random seeds, FID implementation and reference statistics, complete augmentation settings, initialization details, and evaluation protocol are missing. MNG's discriminator interface and aggregation over K noised outputs are ambiguous. More seriously, Eq. 9 defines the REPA loss as positive cosine similarity and Eq. 10 minimizes it with a positive coefficient, which would discourage alignment unless "sim" actually denotes a negated similarity or the displayed sign is wrong.

Originality is moderate rather than high: pure-transformer GANs, latent-space generation, intermediate generator supervision, pretrained-feature assistance, and width-dependent optimization are all established ideas. The particular combination and noise hierarchy are new, but the manuscript overstates novelty by saying transformer GAN scalability had not been discussed, despite citing TransGAN and related work.

Presentation needs substantial polishing. There are frequent grammatical errors, inconsistent symbols and indices in the MNG equations, inconsistent figure numbering (Figure 7 versus references to Figure 6), and unsupported causal language such as claiming a small-sample correlation "proves" scalability. These issues sometimes obstruct technical interpretation rather than being merely cosmetic.

The manuscript contains no explicit limitations or broader-impact/ethics discussion. It should acknowledge dependence on pretrained components, the narrow dataset and resolution, the cost and environmental footprint of the largest experiment, ImageNet and pretrained-model provenance, possible memorization, and misuse risks of efficient image generation. No acute ethical violation is evident, but the treatment is inadequate for the scope of the claims.

Overall, the empirical result is promising and the diagnostics are worthwhile, but unsupported central scaling claims, unfair baseline framing, missing statistical evidence, and consequential reproducibility ambiguities prevent reliable acceptance in the current form. A substantially revised paper could become competitive.

strengths: Soundness: The reported ImageNet-256 results are promising: GAT-XL/2 reaches FID-50K 3.02 without guidance and 2.96 with latent-space guidance after 40 epochs, while the S-to-XL training curves show monotonic improvements with capacity.

The ablations address the proposed components directly. MNG improves FID over no intermediate guidance and resize-based MSG, block-removal LPIPS supports the early-layer-utilization diagnosis, and the cross-scale learning-rate experiment demonstrates a real stability issue.

Significance: A reliable one-step generator with competitive quality would be valuable, particularly given GANs' sampling efficiency. The reported 12-day training run on eight A6000 GPUs is also substantially more accessible than many large generative-model experiments.

Originality: Combining latent-space adversarial training with plain transformer generator and discriminator backbones is a useful synthesis. MNG's noise-ordered intermediate supervision and the simple width-dependent learning-rate rule are practically appealing, even though both build closely on existing ideas.
Presentation: The main architectural ideas, model configurations, learning rates, noise schedule, objectives, compute requirements, and qualitative samples are generally presented clearly.
weaknesses: Soundness: The central scalability claim is supported only on ImageNet-256, with four model configurations and no repeated runs or uncertainty estimates. Width, depth, parameter count, and compute change together, so the four-point GFLOPs correlation of -0.95 is not compelling evidence of a general scaling relationship.

The state-of-the-art and data-efficiency comparisons are not fully controlled. GAT uses a pretrained Stable-Diffusion VAE and frozen DINOv2-B supervision, yet is placed under 'GANs from scratch' while StyleGAN-XL is discounted for pretrained discriminator features. Epoch counts also ignore the substantially different per-step costs of the roughly 1.07B-parameter generator-discriminator pair, DINO feature extraction, and competing methods.

The inverse-width learning-rate rule is only heuristically justified and is evaluated through one S/B cross-swap. There is no learning-rate sweep, comparison with alternatives such as inverse-square-root scaling, or validation of the rule on L/XL, so the experiments show that two transferred rates fail rather than uniquely validating the proposed scaling law.

Evaluation relies almost entirely on FID from a single run. Precision/recall or coverage metrics, memorization checks, and comparisons under matched pretraining and compute would be important for a GAN, especially because the manuscript itself notes that pretrained semantic features can improve FID without proportional perceptual-quality gains. The later 'uncurated' examples additionally use truncation 0.85 and only selected classes.

Reproducibility: Several consequential details are missing or inconsistent, including the exact VAE checkpoint and latent scaling, data preprocessing, DiffAugment policy, learning-rate schedule, AdamW weight decay/epsilon, FID implementation/reference statistics, and random seeds. Equation 9 adds cosine similarity to a minimized discriminator loss, which would discourage alignment unless 'sim' actually denotes negative similarity; this must be corrected or defined.

Presentation and originality: Prior pure-transformer GANs, MSG-GAN, feature-aided GAN training, and latent generative transformers supply most ingredients. The manuscript should narrow its novelty claims and fix ambiguities such as how the K noised images are arranged for the discriminator, whether real and fake branches share noise, and inconsistent Figure 6/7 references.

Limitations and ethics: There is no substantive limitations or broader-impact discussion. The paper should acknowledge the single-dataset/resolution evidence, high training cost, dependence on large pretrained models, ImageNet and foundation-model biases/licensing, and potential misuse of high-quality image generators. These omissions are not by themselves disqualifying, but they weaken the submission's completeness.

Overall, the method and headline result are promising, but the uncontrolled comparisons, narrow and variance-free scaling evidence, and incomplete reproducibility prevent the central claims from being reliable enough for acceptance in the current form. A revision with matched-compute/pretraining comparisons, multiple seeds, broader metrics, and clarified specifications could become strong.

strengths: Soundness/significance: The reported ImageNet-256 result is impressive: GAT-XL/2 reaches FID-50K 2.18 with one function evaluation, alongside favorable CLIP-FID, precision, and recall. The paper also reports useful inference latency and memory measurements.

The empirical study is unusually broad, covering four model scales, patch sizes, decoupled generator/discriminator scaling, ImageNet-512, COCO text-to-image generation, FFHQ unconditional generation, an alternative tokenizer, and large-batch compatibility.

The proposed MNG mechanism is simple and practically motivated. Feature similarity, latent sensitivity, block-removal LPIPS, intermediate visualizations, and FID ablations consistently support the claim that it increases early-layer participation.

Originality: Pure transformer GANs, latent-space generation, multiscale supervision, and representation alignment are individually established, but their combination into a large latent GAN and the diagnosis of early-layer inactivity offer useful new understanding.

Presentation is generally clear, with strong diagrams and extensive appendices. The impact statement appropriately acknowledges synthetic-media misuse and suggests provenance, watermarking, and access-control mitigations.
weaknesses: The central scalability claim is overstated. The power law is fitted to only four summary points, mixes a 100K-iteration XL checkpoint with 50K checkpoints for other sizes, and changes width, depth, learning rate, parameter count, and compute simultaneously. A correlation of -0.95 under these coupled interventions is not strong evidence of a general scaling law or compute-optimal scaling.

The width-aware learning-rate justification analyzes one SGD update of a scalar linear layer on the same input, whereas the actual system uses AdamW, residual transformers, LayerScale, adaptive normalization, and different depths. Empirical validation mainly cross-swaps two learning rates between S and B; it lacks learning-rate sweeps, direct measurements of functional update magnitude, and comparisons with established parameterization/scaling approaches. Thus the claim that the rule reliably eliminates tuning across scales is insufficiently supported.

The headline comparison is not fully transparent or controlled. GAT is placed under “GANs from scratch” despite relying on a pretrained SD-VAE and, crucially, frozen DINOv2 supervision whose ablation changes FID dramatically. The paper criticizes StyleGAN-XL for a pretrained discriminator but does not comparably qualify its own pretrained feature supervision. Epoch counts also obscure that a GAT iteration is reported to cost about five times a DiT iteration, and wall-clock comparisons use different hardware.

The reported 2.18 FID occurs at 60 epochs, but the displayed XL training curve ends at 40 epochs near FID 3.0. At epoch 40 the gradient-penalty coefficient is increased 100-fold, from 0.1 to 10, yet this consequential schedule change is not ablated. Main large-scale results are single runs; the only multi-seed study uses GAT-S for 10 epochs and FID-5K, so it does not establish uncertainty for the headline result.

There are objective and reporting inconsistencies that impede verification. Equation 10 defines REPA as a cosine similarity but adds it positively to a minimized discriminator loss, apparently encouraging anti-alignment unless “sim” actually denotes a distance. Table 6 is captioned as an MNG ablation but contains learning-rate experiments. Equations 1–4 and the architecture do not clearly specify whether multilevel samples are concatenated as channels, tokens, or batch items.

Reproducibility is inadequate for such a large and sensitive system. The project-page field is blank and no code or checkpoint is supplied. The exact FID sampling protocol is unclear, particularly whether truncation or the unexplained latent-space “guidance” mentioned in the appendix is used; data preprocessing, augmentation settings, discriminator update details, and several evaluation choices are also insufficiently specified.

The method is meaningful but largely composes known ingredients: latent-space training, transformer GANs, MSG-style intermediate outputs, DINO representation alignment, and a heuristic learning-rate rescaling. Given the evidential and reproducibility gaps, the promising results do not yet support acceptance, though a revision with controlled scaling experiments, complete evaluation details, corrected objectives, and released code could become strong.

strengths: The paper tackles a significant practical question: whether GANs can retain one-step inference while benefiting from transformer scaling. The reported ImageNet-256 result is strong: GAT-XL/2 reaches FID-50K 2.18 after 60 epochs, alongside favorable CLIP-FID and recall relative to the listed one-step baselines.

The empirical package is broader than a single headline number. It includes S/B/L/XL models, generator-versus-discriminator scaling, patch-size variants, ImageNet-512, text-conditional and unconditional generation, an alternative tokenizer, and several intermediate-feature diagnostics.

The MNG investigation provides useful evidence beyond FID: block-ablation LPIPS, input/output feature similarity, sensitivity to latent noise, and intermediate visualizations consistently indicate increased early-layer activity. Comparing exponential MNG against no MNG, linear MNG, and MSG-style degradation is also informative.

The manuscript is generally well organized and visually polished. Many architectural and optimization details are reported in the appendix, including model dimensions, learning rates, optimizer settings, noise levels, parameter counts, and training cost. The impact statement acknowledges synthetic-media misuse and suggests provenance, watermarking, and access controls.
weaknesses: The central claim of a scaling law is not adequately supported. The power law is fitted to only four endpoint observations, with XL evaluated at 100K iterations while the other sizes use 50K, and no uncertainty, held-out prediction, alternative functional fit, or repeated runs is provided. A correlation over closely related configurations is insufficient to establish genuine scaling behavior, particularly because width, depth, parameter count, learning rate, and compute change together.

The proposed width-aware learning-rate rule is justified using a one-layer scalar-output SGD calculation evaluated on the same input, but the actual system is a deep residual transformer trained with AdamW. The argument assumes that the loss gradient is width-independent and ignores parameterization, attention, depth, residual scaling, and optimizer normalization. Empirically, only reciprocal S/B learning-rate transfers are tested; there are no learning-rate sweeps or corresponding controls for L/XL, so the evidence shows that two learning rates are not interchangeable rather than validating the claimed inverse-width rule.

The strongest comparison is not fully controlled. GAT uses a pretrained SD VAE and frozen DINOv2-B supervision, yet Table 1 groups it under models trained 'from scratch.' REPA has an exceptionally large effect—for example, FID-5K improves from 38.99 to 22.08 for GAT-S at 20 epochs—so comparisons should separate the contribution of external pretrained representations and include similarly equipped baselines. Epoch count is also a weak efficiency measure when the appendix reports each GAT iteration is roughly five times as expensive as a DiT iteration.

Important evaluation details remain unclear, including whether truncation or other latent-space guidance is used for the reported FID, the exact FID/precision/recall implementation and reference statistics, and the full differentiable-augmentation configuration. The project-page field is blank and no code or checkpoints are supplied, limiting reproducibility of an expensive system.

There are objective-level ambiguities. Equation 10 defines the REPA loss as positive similarity and Equation 11 adds it to a minimized discriminator loss, which would encourage anti-alignment unless a negative sign or maximization convention is intended. Equations 1–9 are also unclear about whether multilevel samples are concatenated along the batch, channel, or token dimension and how discriminator logits are aggregated. These are material implementation details rather than cosmetic notation issues.

MNG's coarse-to-fine interpretation is stronger than the evidence supports. Isotropic Gaussian corruption reduces signal-to-noise ratio but does not explicitly isolate spatial frequency or coarse structure. The diagnostics establish that early blocks change outputs more, but not that this additional activity is useful capacity rather than sensitivity induced by auxiliary heads. Comparisons with parameter- or compute-matched deep baselines and alternative intermediate supervision would strengthen the causal claim.

Reported uncertainty is inadequate for adversarial training. The only multi-seed experiment uses the smallest model, just 10 epochs, and FID-5K; its scores range from 28.907 to 31.157. Main FID-50K results, ablations, the 2.18 headline result, and the four-point scaling fit appear to be single runs, so differences and stability claims cannot be assessed reliably.

Originality is moderate rather than high: latent-space generation, transformer GANs, multilevel discriminator supervision, pretrained-feature assistance, and learning-rate scaling heuristics all have close precedents. The particular combination and early-layer analysis are useful, but the manuscript overstates them as evidence that GAN scalability has been established. Writing also contains several grammatical errors, duplicated references, inconsistent notation, and unsupported causal language such as claiming the plots 'prove' scalability. The ethics discussion is reasonable but generic and does not address ImageNet data provenance or representational harms.

strengths: Soundness: The main empirical result is strong: GAT-XL/2 achieves FID-50K 2.18 on class-conditional ImageNet-256 with one function evaluation, alongside CLIP-FID 1.86 and improved recall, reducing concern that the gain is merely an Inception-feature artifact.

Soundness: The paper supports its design with useful diagnostics and ablations. MNG is examined through intermediate-feature PCA, block removal with LPIPS over 10K images, feature-change and latent-sensitivity measurements, and comparisons against no MNG, linear noise scheduling, and MSG-style supervision. Separate generator/discriminator scaling and REPA ablations add further insight.

Significance: A competitive single-pass generator is practically valuable. The reported 0.0773 seconds per image versus 15.2612 for a 250-step DiT, together with strong generation quality, makes the contribution relevant beyond a purely architectural study.

Originality: Combining latent-space transformer GANs, noise-perturbed intermediate adversarial supervision, and a width-aware learning-rate rule forms a coherent contribution. The early-layer underutilization analysis provides useful understanding even though several ingredients build on prior work.

Breadth: Results cover four model scales, two patch sizes, ImageNet-512, an alternative tokenizer, large-batch training, unconditional FFHQ, and a preliminary text-to-image extension. Qualitative examples and latent editing experiments further demonstrate model utility.

Presentation: The central motivation, architecture, and coarse-to-fine role of MNG are generally clear, and the appendix contains model configurations, learning rates, noise levels, training cost, and additional analyses.

Limitations and ethics: The authors honestly disclose the limited multi-seed evaluation and substantial training cost. The impact statement appropriately identifies synthetic-media misuse and suggests provenance, watermarking, and access-control mitigations.
weaknesses: The central scalability claim is broader than the evidence. The claimed power law is fitted to only four summary points, mixes the XL result at 100K iterations with the other models at 50K, provides no held-out prediction, and does not separate the effects of parameter count, training compute, and discriminator capacity. It demonstrates favorable scaling over the tested range, but not yet a robust scaling law.

The width-aware learning-rate justification is heuristic: it analyzes one SGD update of a scalar linear layer on the same input, whereas the experiments use AdamW in deep residual transformers and vary depth as well as width. The decisive cross-learning-rate control is shown only for S and B; corresponding controls for L and XL or direct measurements of functional update magnitude would better support the stated mechanism and generality.

Statistical evidence is limited. Most principal and ablation results appear to be single runs. The only multi-seed study uses GAT-S/2 for 10 epochs and FID-5K, with scores from 28.907 to 31.157; this is not sufficient to quantify uncertainty in the small 2.30-to-2.18 state-of-the-art margin at XL scale.

The strongest components are mainly ablated on small models and sometimes with FID-5K rather than the headline FID-50K. In particular, there is no full factorial or large-scale ablation establishing how much of the XL result comes from MNG, the learning-rate rule, REPA, the modern GAN objective, and the other architectural/training choices.

Reproducibility is not yet adequate for an unqualified accept: the project-page field is blank and no code or checkpoints are provided. Important details remain unclear or absent, including the exact SD-VAE checkpoint and latent normalization, differentiable-augmentation policy, AdamW weight decay, ImageNet preprocessing, and the precise sampling/truncation or guidance settings used for reported quantitative metrics.

There are several consequential presentation inconsistencies. Table 6 is labeled as an MNG ablation but contains the adaptive-learning-rate cross-check results. Equation 10 defines the REPA term as positive similarity and Equation 11 minimizes it, apparently encouraging lower similarity unless an unstated negative-similarity convention is intended. The notation for intermediate outputs and perturbed counterparts is also occasionally inconsistent.

Some efficiency comparisons are not fully controlled. Parameter counts in the headline table appear to report the 602M generator while training additionally uses a 468M discriminator and a frozen DINOv2 teacher. Epoch counts establish data passes but do not by themselves establish compute efficiency; the paper acknowledges that each GAT step is roughly five times slower than a DiT-style step.

The evaluation remains centered on FID-style aggregate metrics and curated tasks. Precision/recall and CLIP-FID help, but human evaluation or stronger tests of class fidelity, memorization, and rare-mode behavior would make the quality claim more convincing. The text-to-image and unconditional experiments are useful but comparatively preliminary.
